{{Short description|Subgroup of an abelian group consisting of all elements of finite order}}
In the theory of [[abelian group]]s, the '''torsion subgroup''' <math>A_T</math> of an abelian group <math>A</math> is the [[subgroup]] of <math>A</math> consisting of all elements that have finite [[order (group theory)|order]] (the '''torsion elements''' of <math>A</math>).<ref>{{citation | last=Serge|first = Lang  
|authorlink=Serge Lang
| title = Algebra
|pages=42 
|edition=3rd
| publisher = Addison-Wesley 
| year = 1993 
| isbn = 0-201-55540-9}}</ref> An abelian group <math>A</math> is called a [[torsion group]] (or periodic group) if every element of <math>A</math> has finite order and is called [[Torsion-free abelian group|torsion-free]] if every element of <math>A</math> except the [[identity element|identity]] is of infinite order.

The proof that <math>A_T</math> is closed under the group operation relies on the commutativity of the operation (see examples section).

If <math>A</math> is abelian, then the torsion subgroup <math>T</math> is a [[characteristic subgroup|fully characteristic subgroup]] of <math>A</math> and the factor group <math>A/T</math> is torsion-free. There is a [[covariant functor]] from the [[category of abelian groups]] to the category of torsion groups that sends every group to its torsion subgroup and every [[Group homomorphism|homomorphism]] to its restriction to the torsion subgroup. There is another covariant functor from the category of abelian groups to the category of torsion-free groups that sends every group to its quotient by its torsion subgroup, and sends every homomorphism to the obvious induced homomorphism (which is easily seen to be well-defined).

If <math>A</math> is [[finitely generated group|finitely generated]] and abelian, then it can be written as the [[direct sum of groups|direct sum]] of its torsion subgroup <math>T</math> and a torsion-free subgroup (but this is not true for all infinitely generated abelian groups). In any decomposition of <math>A</math> as a direct sum of a torsion subgroup <math>S</math> and a torsion-free subgroup, <math>S</math> must equal <math>T</math> (but the torsion-free subgroup is not uniquely determined). This is a key step in the classification of [[finitely generated abelian group]]s.

==<math>p</math>-power torsion subgroups==
For any abelian group <math>(A, +)</math> and any [[prime number]] <math>p</math> the set <math>A_{T_p}</math> of elements of <math>A</math> that have order a power of <math>p</math> is a subgroup called the ''' <math>p</math>-power torsion subgroup'''  or, more loosely, the ''' <math>p</math>-torsion subgroup''':

:<math>A_{T_p}=\{a\in A \;|\; \exists n\in \mathbb{N}\;, p^n a = 0\}.\;</math>

The torsion subgroup <math>A_T</math> is isomorphic to the direct sum of its <math>p</math>-power torsion subgroups over all prime numbers <math>p</math>:

:<math>A_T \cong \bigoplus_{p\in P} A_{T_p}.\;</math>

When <math>A</math> is a finite abelian group, <math>A_{T_p}</math> coincides with the unique [[Sylow subgroup|Sylow <math>p</math>-subgroup]] of <math>A</math>.

Each <math>p</math>-power torsion subgroup of <math>A</math> is a [[characteristic subgroup|fully characteristic subgroup]]. More strongly, any homomorphism between abelian groups sends each <math>p</math>-power torsion subgroup into the corresponding <math>p</math>-power torsion subgroup.

For each prime number <math>p</math>, this provides a [[functor]] from the category of abelian groups to the category of <math>p</math>-power torsion groups that sends every group to its <math>p</math>-power torsion subgroup, and restricts every homomorphism to the <math>p</math>-torsion subgroups. The product over the set of all prime numbers of the restriction of these functors to the category of torsion groups, is a [[faithful functor]] from the category of torsion groups to the product over all prime numbers of the categories of <math>p</math>-torsion groups. In a sense, this means that studying <math>p</math>-torsion groups in isolation tells us everything about torsion groups in general.

==Examples and further results==
[[Image:Lattice torsion points.svg|right|thumb|200px|The 4-torsion subgroup of the quotient group of the complex numbers under addition by a lattice.]]

*The torsion subset of a non-abelian group is not, in general, a subgroup. For example, in the [[infinite dihedral group]], which has [[presentation of a group|presentation]]
:<math>\langle x,y \mid x^2=y^2=1 \rangle </math>,
:the element <math>xy</math> is a product of two torsion elements, but has infinite order.

* The torsion elements in a [[nilpotent group]] form a [[normal subgroup]].<ref>{{Cite book |last=Epstein |first=David B. A. |title=Word Processing in Groups |last2=Cannon |first2=James W. |last3=Holt |first3=Derek F. |last4=Levy |first4=Silvio V. F. |last5=Paterson |first5=Mike |last6=Thurston |first6=William |collaboration= |publisher=Jones and Bartlett |year=1992 |isbn=0-86720-244-0 |pages=167}}</ref>

*Every finite abelian group is a torsion group. Not every torsion group is finite however: consider the direct sum of a [[countably infinite|countable]] number of copies of the [[cyclic group]] <math>C_2</math>; this is a torsion group since every element has order 2. Nor need there be an upper bound on the orders of elements in a torsion group if it isn't [[generating set of a group|finitely generated]], as the example of the [[factor group]] <math>\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}</math> shows.

*Every [[free abelian group]] is torsion-free, but the converse is not true, as is shown by the additive group of the [[rational number]]s <math>\mathbb{Q}</math>.

*Even if <math>A</math> is not finitely generated, the ''size'' of its torsion-free part is uniquely determined, as is explained in more detail in the article on [[rank of an abelian group]].
*An abelian group <math>A</math> is torsion-free [[if and only if]] it is [[flat module|flat]] as a <math>\Z</math>-[[module (mathematics)|module]], which means that whenever <math>C</math> is a subgroup of some abelian group <math>B</math>, then the natural map from the [[tensor product of abelian groups|tensor product]] <math>C\otimes A\to B\otimes A</math> is [[injective]].

*Tensoring an abelian group <math>A</math> with <math>\mathbb{Q}</math> (or any [[divisible group]]) kills torsion. That is, if <math>T</math> is a torsion group then <math>T\otimes\mathbb{Q}=0</math>. For a general abelian group <math>A</math> with torsion subgroup <math>T</math> one has <math>A\otimes\mathbb{Q}\cong A/T\otimes\mathbb{Q}</math>.

*Taking the torsion subgroup makes torsion abelian groups into a [[coreflective subcategory]] of abelian groups, while taking the quotient by the torsion subgroup makes torsion-free abelian groups into a [[reflective subcategory]].
